main.title: How a computer works
main.why: every abstraction you use (JS, Docker, Kubernetes) is eventually a CPU executing instructions on bytes in memory.

mustKnow.t: Information as bits
c: Binary, decimal, hexadecimal; converting between them by hand
Bits, bytes, words; KB vs KiB
Signed integers and two's complement; overflow
Floating point (IEEE 754) and why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3
Text encoding: ASCII, Unicode, code points, UTF-8 vs UTF-16

mustKnow.t: Logic and hardware
c: Logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, XOR) and how they build an adder
The CPU: registers, ALU, control unit, clock speed
The fetch-decode-execute cycle
Instruction sets (x86, ARM) and machine code vs assembly

mustKnow.t: Memory
c: Memory hierarchy: registers → L1/L2/L3 cache → RAM → SSD/disk → network
Approximate latencies at each level ("latency numbers every programmer should know")
Addresses and pointers; what "a value lives at an address" means

mustKnow.t: From source code to running program
c: Compiler, interpreter, JIT compiler; what each does
Source → assembly → object file → linker → executable

niche: Endianness (big vs little endian) and why network protocols care
Cache lines (64 bytes) and why iterating an array row-by-row is faster than column-by- column
Branch prediction and why sorted data can make loops faster
Unicode normalization and grapheme clusters (why emoji "length" is weird in JS)
Integer overflow bugs in real systems (Ariane 5, Y2038)

resources.text: Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software (Charles Petzold, 2nd ed.) — read chapters on number systems, logic gates, adders, memory and the CPU; skim the rest
CS50 (Harvard, free on edX/YouTube) Week 0-1 lectures for a gentle start
Crash Course Computer Science (YouTube), episodes 1-10
"Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know" (search it; many versions)

checklist.text: Petzold, number systems + binary chapters. Convert 10 numbers between binary/decimal/hex by hand.
Petzold, logic gates + adders. Draw a half adder and full adder on paper.
Petzold, memory + CPU chapters, or Crash Course CS episodes 5-9.
Write a tiny C program, compile it with gcc -S, and read the generated assembly. Write your first note: "What happens when I run a program".

main.doneWhen: you can explain, with a drawing, how a CPU runs one instruction, and why reading from RAM is ~100x slower than from L1 cache.

main.title: Operating systems I — processes, threads, memory
main.why: your Node server, your browser tabs and your Docker containers are all processes. You need to know what that means.

mustKnow.t: What an OS is: the kernel, user mode vs kernel mode
Processes
c: A process = program + memory + state; the PCB (process control block)
Process states (running, ready, blocked)
fork(), exec(), wait(); parent and child processes; PIDs
Context switching and its cost

mustKnow.t: CPU scheduling: time slices, round robin, priorities, why your app "pauses"
Memory
c: Virtual memory and address spaces; why each process thinks it owns all memory
Pages, page tables, the TLB, page faults
A process's memory layout: code, data, heap, stack
Stack vs heap: what goes where, stack overflow, memory leaks

mustKnow.t: Threads
c: Threads vs processes: what's shared and what isn't
Concurrency vs parallelism

niche: Copy-on-write after fork() (why forking is cheap)
Zombie and orphan processes
Swap and thrashing; the Linux OOM killer (why your container gets "OOMKilled")
Memory-mapped files (mmap)
Green threads / user-space threads vs OS threads (relevant to Go, Java virtual threads)

resources.text: OSTEP: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (free) — chapters 4-6 (processes, process API, limited direct execution), 7 (scheduling intro), 13-16 and 18 (address spaces, memory API, address translation, segmentation, paging intro), 26 (concurrency intro)
Julia Evans' zines on Linux and processes (wizardzines.com)

checklist.text: OSTEP ch. 4-5. Run ps aux and top; find the PID of your browser.
OSTEP ch. 6-7. Write down what a context switch saves and restores.
OSTEP ch. 13-16, 18. Draw a process's memory layout from memory.
In C: write a program that fork() s, prints both PIDs, and wait() s. Then a program that recurses until stack overflow. Then read OSTEP ch. 26.

main.doneWhen: you can explain what a process is, why two processes can't read each other's memory, and the difference between a process and a thread.

main.title: Operating systems II — files, syscalls, I/O, concurrency
main.why: every file read, network request and log line in your app is a system call. Concurrency bugs are the hardest bugs you'll face.

mustKnow.t: System calls: the boundary between your code and the kernel; strace
Files and file systems
c: Everything-is-a-file; file descriptors (0, 1, 2 = stdin, stdout, stderr)
open, read, write, close; inodes, directories, hard vs soft links
Buffering: why write doesn't always hit the disk; fsync

mustKnow.t: I/O models
c: Blocking vs non-blocking I/O
I/O multiplexing: select, poll, epoll (the foundation of Node.js and NGINX)

mustKnow.t: Concurrency
c: Race conditions and critical sections
Locks/mutexes, condition variables, semaphores
Deadlock: the four conditions and how to avoid it

mustKnow.t: Inter-process communication: pipes, signals, sockets, shared memory

niche: epoll vs kqueue vs io_uring (how modern servers do async I/O)
File descriptor limits (ulimit -n) and "too many open files" in production
Atomic operations and compare-and-swap (CAS)
The thundering herd problem
Signals: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL vs SIGINT (why graceful shutdown matters in Kubernetes)

resources.text: OSTEP chapters 28-32 (locks, condition variables, semaphores, concurrency bugs), 33 (event-based concurrency — read twice, it's Node.js), 39-40 (files and directories, file system implementation)
Julia Evans' strace zine

checklist.text: OSTEP ch. 39. Run strace cat somefile and identify every syscall.
OSTEP ch. 28-30. Write down a race condition example in your own words.
OSTEP ch. 31-33. Note how event-based concurrency differs from threads.
In Java, C or Python: two threads incrementing a shared counter 1M times without a lock (see the wrong result), then with a lock. Then strace a Node.js script that reads a file.

main.doneWhen: you can explain what a file descriptor is, why a race condition happens, and how one thread can handle thousands of connections with epoll.

main.title: Linux and the shell
main.why: every server you deploy to is Linux. Being slow in the terminal makes every later topic slower.

mustKnow.t: The filesystem layout: /, /etc, /var, /usr, /home, /tmp, /proc, /dev
Navigation and files: ls, cd, cp, mv, rm, find, cat, less, head, tail -f
Permissions: users, groups, rwx, octal (755, 644), chmod, chown, sudo, root
Shell fundamentals
c: The shell is a program; bash vs zsh
Environment variables, PATH, export,.bashrc
Pipes and redirection: |, >, >>, 2>&1
Exit codes, &&, ||

mustKnow.t: Text processing: grep, sed, awk, sort, uniq, wc, cut, xargs, jq
Processes from the shell: ps, top / htop, kill, jobs, &, nohup
Networking from the shell: curl, ping, ss / netstat, lsof -i, dig, ssh, scp
Package managers (apt), services (systemctl), logs (journalctl)
Shell scripting basics: variables, conditionals, loops, functions, shebang

niche: /proc as a live window into the kernel (/proc/<pid>/status, /proc/cpuinfo)
SSH keys, ~/.ssh/config, agent forwarding, port forwarding/tunnels
tmux for sessions that survive disconnects
Cron syntax (you'll see it again in Kubernetes CronJobs)
set -euo pipefail in scripts and why it prevents silent failures

resources.text: MIT Missing Semester — lectures 1-5 (shell, scripting, editors, data wrangling, command-line environment)
The Linux Command Line by William Shotts (free PDF at linuxcommand.org)
OverTheWire Bandit — a game that teaches Linux by doing

checklist.text: Missing Semester lecture 1-2 + exercises. If on Windows, install WSL2 Ubuntu first.
Missing Semester lecture 4 (data wrangling). Use grep / awk / sort on a real log file.
Missing Semester lecture 5. Explore /proc for a running process.
OverTheWire Bandit levels 0-15. Write a backup script with timestamps and set - euo pipefail.

main.doneWhen: you can find which process is using port 3000, kill it, and write a script that greps errors out of a log and counts them, without searching the web.

main.title: Git, from the inside
main.why: you use Git daily. Once you see it's just a small database of snapshots, merge conflicts and rebases stop being scary.

mustKnow.t: The object model
c: Blobs (file contents), trees (directories), commits (snapshot + parent + message), tags
Content addressing: every object is named by the hash of its content
The.git folder: objects/, refs/, HEAD, index

mustKnow.t: Refs: a branch is a file containing a commit hash; HEAD points to a branch; detached HEAD
The three areas: working directory, index (staging area), repository
Operations, explained by what they do to the graph
c: commit, branch, checkout / switch, merge (fast-forward vs three-way), rebase, cherry-pick, reset (soft/mixed/hard), revert, stash
Remotes: fetch vs pull, push, tracking branches, origin/main

mustKnow.t: Undoing mistakes safely with reflog
Team workflows: feature branches, pull requests, trunk-based development, conventional commits

niche: Packfiles and delta compression (why.git stays small)
git bisect to find which commit introduced a bug
git blame -w -C and git log -S (pickaxe search)
Interactive rebase (rebase -i) for clean history; --fixup and --autosquash
Signed commits;.gitattributes; Git hooks (pre-commit)
SHA-1 to SHA-256 transition

resources.text: Pro Git book (free) — chapters 2, 3 and 10 (Git Internals)
Learn Git Branching — interactive visual exercises
Mary Rose Cook's essay Git from the inside out

checklist.text: Pro Git ch. 10.1-10.3 (objects, refs). Open.git/ in a repo and find a commit object.
Learn Git Branching, the "Main" levels.
Pro Git ch. 3 (branching). Practice merge vs rebase on a toy repo and draw the graph each time.
Create a commit by hand with git hash-object -w, git update-index, git write-tree, git commit-tree, git update-ref. Then use git bisect on a toy repo with a planted bug.

main.doneWhen: you can explain what a branch physically is on disk, and what rebase does to commit hashes and why.

main.title: Networking — IP, TCP, UDP, DNS
main.why: every API call, every database query and every Kubernetes service is network traffic. Most production mysteries are network mysteries.

mustKnow.t: Layered models: OSI (7 layers) vs TCP/IP (4 layers); encapsulation
Link layer: MAC addresses, Ethernet, Wi-Fi, ARP, switches
Network layer (IP)
c: IPv4 addresses, IPv6 basics
Subnets and CIDR notation (10.0.0.0/16), private IP ranges
Routers, routing tables, default gateway, TTL, traceroute
NAT and why your laptop's IP isn't your public IP

mustKnow.t: Transport layer
c: Ports and sockets (IP + port + protocol)
TCP: three-way handshake, sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmission, flow control (window), congestion control (slow start), four-way close, TIME_WAIT
UDP: when it's better than TCP (DNS, video, games, QUIC)

mustKnow.t: DNS
c: The hierarchy: root → TLD → authoritative servers; recursive resolvers
Record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SRV
TTLs and caching at every level

mustKnow.t: DHCP: how your device gets an IP
Sockets API: socket, bind, listen, accept, connect

niche: Head-of-line blocking in TCP (and why HTTP/3 moved to UDP)
Nagle's algorithm and TCP_NODELAY
MTU, fragmentation and path MTU discovery
Ephemeral port exhaustion under high load
0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1 binding (why your Docker container "isn't reachable")
Anycast (how CDNs and 8.8.8.8 work)
BGP at a high level: how the internet's networks find each other

resources.text: High Performance Browser Networking by Ilya Grigorik (free) — chapters 1-3 (latency, TCP, UDP)
Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (Kurose & Ross) — chapters 1, 3 and 4 as reference; Kurose's own lecture videos are free on YouTube
Julia Evans' Networking! ACK! zine and her post on how DNS works
Beej's Guide to Network Programming (free)

checklist.text: Kurose ch. 1 (or videos). Run ip addr, ip route, traceroute google.com; explain each line.
HPBN ch. 1-2. Draw the TCP handshake and slow start.
DNS: Julia Evans' post + dig +trace example.com. Write down every server queried.

Build a TCP echo server and client in Java (ServerSocket and Socket, from your Java track), or with Node's net module if you already know JavaScript. Capture the traffic in Wireshark; find SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK and FIN.

main.doneWhen: you can explain everything that happens between pressing Enter and the first byte of a TCP connection being sent, including DNS.

main.title: HTTP and TLS
main.why: HTTP is the language of everything you build. You'll write a server that speaks it with no framework.

mustKnow.t: HTTP/1.1 message anatomy: request line, headers, blank line, body; status line
Methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS; safe vs idempotent
Headers: Host, Content-Type, Content-Length, Accept, Authorization, User- Agent, Location
Cookies: Set-Cookie, attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Domain, Path, Max-Age)
Caching: Cache-Control (max-age, no-cache vs no-store, public/private, immutable), ETag / If-None-Match, Last-Modified, Vary
Connection management: keep-alive, chunked transfer encoding, compression (gzip, brotli)
HTTP/2 (binary framing, multiplexing, header compression) and HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP)
CORS: same-origin policy, simple vs preflight requests, Access-Control-Allow-* headers
TLS
c: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption, hashing, digital signatures
The TLS 1.3 handshake; certificates, chains of trust, certificate authorities
What HTTPS protects (content, integrity) and what it doesn't (the domain via SNI, timing)

niche: 502 vs 503 vs 504: which component is failing (you'll see these from NGINX)
Vary header and cache poisoning
HSTS and preload lists
Certificate pinning, OCSP stapling, Let's Encrypt and the ACME protocol
HTTP request smuggling (why proxies must agree on Content-Length)
TLS session resumption and 0-RTT
Range requests (how video seeking and resumable downloads work)

resources.text: MDN HTTP guide — Overview, Messages, Caching, Cookies, CORS, Redirections
HPBN chapters 4 (TLS), 9-12 (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2)
The Illustrated TLS 1.3 Connection — every byte of a handshake explained
CodeCrafters "Build your own HTTP server" (optional guided version)

checklist.text: MDN Overview + Messages. Use curl -v on 5 sites and read every header.
MDN Caching + Cookies + CORS. Explain no-cache vs no-store in your notes.
HPBN ch. 4 + Illustrated TLS 1.3. Open a site's certificate in your browser and trace its chain.

Build an HTTP/1.1 server on raw TCP (Java ServerSocket or Node net; no HTTP library): parse requests, serve static files with correct Content-Type, 404s, keep-alive, and an ETag - based 304. Test with curl -v and a browser.

main.doneWhen: your server serves a real HTML page to a browser, and you can explain the full journey: DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP request → response.

main.title: How the browser renders a page
main.why: HTML, CSS and JS only make sense once you know the machine that runs them.

mustKnow.t: Browser architecture: browser process, renderer processes, GPU process, network service; site isolation
Navigation: URL parsing, the network request, response, commit, and the renderer taking over
The critical rendering path
c: Bytes → characters → tokens → nodes → DOM
CSS → CSSOM; why CSS is render-blocking
Render tree (DOM + CSSOM, minus hidden nodes)
Layout (reflow): computing geometry
Paint: filling pixels into layers
Compositing: layers combined on the GPU

mustKnow.t: How scripts affect parsing: blocking <script>, async, defer, type="module"; the preload scanner
The main thread: why one long JS task freezes everything
Using DevTools: Elements, Network (waterfall), Performance (flame chart), Lighthouse

niche: Layout thrashing (forced synchronous layout) from reading offsetHeight after writes
What creates a compositor layer (transform, opacity, will-change) and the cost of too many layers
The back/forward cache (bfcache)
Resource hints: preload, prefetch, preconnect, dns-prefetch, fetchpriority
requestAnimationFrame and the 16.6 ms frame budget

resources.text: Inside look at modern web browser (Mariko Kosaka, 4 parts)
How browsers work (Tali Garsiel, on web.dev) — long; read the parsing and render tree sections
Critical rendering path on MDN

checklist.text: Inside look, parts 1-2.
Inside look, parts 3-4. Draw the pipeline DOM → CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite.
How browsers work (parsing + render tree sections).
Serve a page from your Week 7 server. Record a Performance trace in DevTools and label every phase. Add a blocking script, then defer it, and compare the traces.

main.doneWhen: you can explain why a <script> in the <head> without defer slows the page, and what happens between HTML arriving and pixels appearing.

main.title: HTML and accessibility
main.why: HTML is the structure everything else hangs on, and most developers have never learned it properly.

mustKnow.t: Document structure: doctype, <html>, <head> (meta charset, viewport, title, link, script), <body>
Semantic elements: header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer, headings hierarchy
Text, lists, links (absolute vs relative URLs), images (alt, srcset, sizes, loading="lazy"), picture, video/audio
Tables done right (thead, th scope, caption)
Forms in depth: form action / method, input types, label, name, fieldset, built-in validation, how a form submits without JS (URL-encoded vs multipart)
Block vs inline elements
Accessibility: the accessibility tree, semantic HTML first, ARIA roles/states (and the first rule of ARIA: don't use it if HTML can do it), keyboard navigation, focus management, color contrast
SEO basics: title, meta description, Open Graph, canonical URLs, structured data

niche: <button> vs <div onclick> and why it matters for keyboards and screen readers
<dialog>, <details> / <summary>, popover attribute: native components with no JS
inert attribute and focus traps
HTML parsing error recovery (why broken HTML still renders)
Character references and the XSS danger of injecting HTML
<template> and Web Components / Shadow DOM basics

web.dev Learn Accessibility
MDN HTML reference for each element as needed

checklist.text: Learn HTML modules 1-8.
Learn HTML modules on forms and images.
Learn Accessibility, first half. Turn on your OS screen reader and use a website for 10 minutes.
Build a 3-page site (home, article, contact form) in pure semantic HTML. Make the form submit to your Week 7 server and parse the URL-encoded body. Run a Lighthouse accessibility audit; reach 100.

main.doneWhen: a form on your page submits to your own server with no JavaScript, and the page is fully usable with only a keyboard.

main.title: CSS I — the cascade, box model, flow and stacking
main.why: CSS feels random only when you don't know its rules. It has very few, and they're strict.

mustKnow.t: How CSS is applied: selectors, the cascade (origin, importance, specificity, order), inheritance, initial/inherit/unset
Specificity calculation by hand
Computed values and the DevTools Computed panel
The box model: content, padding, border, margin; box-sizing
Margin collapsing
Normal flow: block and inline formatting contexts; display values
Units: px, em, rem, %, vw / vh, ch; absolute vs relative
Positioning: static, relative, absolute (containing block!), fixed, sticky
Stacking contexts and z-index: what creates a stacking context
Overflow, floats (legacy, but you'll meet them)
Colors, typography, line-height, web fonts and font-display

niche: Block formatting contexts (BFC) and why display: flow-root fixes weird layouts
Cascade layers (@layer) for managing specificity in big codebases
Logical properties (margin-inline-start) for right-to-left languages
CSS custom properties (variables) are inherited and live at runtime, unlike Sass variables
:is(),:where() (zero specificity) and:has() (the "parent selector")

resources.text: web.dev Learn CSS — modules 1-12 this week
Josh Comeau's blog posts on the box model, stacking contexts and positioning (his CSS for JavaScript Developers course is excellent if budget allows)
Specificity calculator

Learn CSS: inheritance, color, sizing units, layout intro.
Positioning and z-index; Josh Comeau's stacking context post.

main.title: CSS II — Flexbox, Grid, responsive, performance
main.why: modern layout is Flexbox and Grid. With them plus Week 10's rules, you can build any layout.

mustKnow.t: Flexbox: main/cross axis, flex-grow / shrink / basis, wrapping, alignment, gap, ordering
Grid: tracks, fr, repeat, minmax, auto-fit vs auto-fill, named areas, implicit vs explicit grid, alignment
When to use Flexbox vs Grid
Responsive design: mobile-first, media queries, fluid typography with clamp(), responsive images
Container queries
Transitions and animations; which properties are cheap to animate (transform, opacity) and why (Week 8's compositing)
Design systems basics: spacing scales, tokens
How Tailwind and CSS-in-JS work underneath (they generate ordinary CSS)

Subgrid
prefers-reduced-motion and prefers-color-scheme
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) caused by images without dimensions and late-loading fonts
content-visibility: auto for rendering performance
How CSS-in-JS can cost runtime performance compared with static CSS

Josh Comeau's An Interactive Guide to Flexbox and An Interactive Guide to CSS Grid

Grid Garden + Josh Comeau's Grid guide.

main.title: JavaScript, the language I
main.why: frameworks come and go; the language underneath them stays. By now your Java track has taught you programming basics, so JS will feel familiar.

Primitives vs references: copying, comparing, mutating; pass-by-value-of-reference
Type coercion: == vs ===, truthy/falsy, the abstract equality algorithm at a high level
Variables: var vs let vs const; block vs function scope; the temporal dead zone
Hoisting: what is really hoisted and why
Functions: declarations vs expressions vs arrows; first-class functions; higher-order functions; default and rest parameters
Scope chain and lexical scope
Closures: what they capture, the classic loop bug, uses (private state, memoization, factories)
Objects: literals, property descriptors, getters/setters, spread, destructuring, optional chaining, nullish coalescing
Arrays: map / filter / reduce / find / some / every / flatMap, mutating vs non- mutating methods
Strings and template literals; Number precision; BigInt

Property enumeration order rules
Object.freeze is shallow; structuredClone for deep copies
Tagged template literals (how styled-components and graphql tags work)
Labels and break label (rare but real)
Strict mode and what it changes

Promise states, chaining, Promise.all / allSettled / race / any

Proxy and Reflect (how Vue's reactivity works)

Same-origin policy for storage; storage partitioning
Structural typing in TypeScript (vs Java's nominal typing — compare with your Java track)
Declaration files (.d.ts) and how npm packages ship types
Conditional and mapped types; satisfies

main.title: Containers and Docker

What a container really is

mustKnow.t: Containers vs VMs (shared kernel vs hypervisor)

main.title: Kubernetes I — the model and core objects
main.why: Kubernetes is a control loop that keeps reality matching a YAML file. Learn that idea and the objects stop being a vocabulary list.

mustKnow.t: The problem: running many containers on many machines, restarting failures, scaling, rolling out new versions
Declarative desired state + reconciliation loops (controllers compare desired vs actual and act)
Architecture
c: Control plane: API server, etcd (the cluster's database), scheduler, controller manager
Nodes: kubelet, container runtime (containerd), kube-proxy

mustKnow.t: Core objects
c: Pod (one or more containers sharing network and storage), pod lifecycle
ReplicaSet, Deployment (rolling updates, rollbacks), StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob
Service: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer; how Services get stable IPs and DNS names; Endpoints/EndpointSlices
ConfigMap and Secret (and that Secrets are only base64 by default)
Namespaces, labels and selectors

mustKnow.t: Probes: liveness, readiness, startup (your Week 21 health endpoints)
Resource requests vs limits; QoS classes; OOMKilled (Week 2)
kubectl: get, describe, logs, exec, apply, port-forward, rollout

niche: Graceful shutdown in Kubernetes: preStop hooks, SIGTERM, terminationGracePeriodSeconds, and the race with endpoint removal

Ingress: an object describing HTTP routing (hosts, paths, TLS) into Services

Storage: Volumes, PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses
Autoscaling: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, cluster autoscaler
Packaging: Helm charts, Kustomize

main.title: Distributed data — replication and partitioning
main.why: the moment data lives on more than one machine, every "simple" guarantee becomes a tradeoff.

mustKnow.t: Why distribute: scalability, availability, latency (geo)
Vertical vs horizontal scaling; stateless services scale easily, data doesn't
Replication
c: Leader-follower: sync vs async, replication lag, read-your-writes, monotonic reads
Failover and split brain
Multi-leader and leaderless (quorums: W + R > N); conflict resolution, last-write- wins, CRDTs at a concept level

mustKnow.t: Partitioning (sharding)
c: By key range vs by hash; hot spots; consistent hashing (you'll implement it in the DSA track)
Secondary indexes across partitions (local vs global)
Rebalancing and request routing

mustKnow.t: Back-of-envelope estimation: QPS, storage per year, bandwidth, memory for cache; powers of two; latency numbers from Week 1

niche: Clock problems: why you can't trust timestamps across machines; logical clocks (Lamport), vector clocks
Read replicas returning stale data right after a user's write
Cross-shard transactions and why they're avoided
Tail latency amplification with fan-out

main.title: Consistency, consensus and messaging patterns
main.why: this is the theory behind "why is distributed systems hard", plus the patterns that make microservices survivable.

mustKnow.t: Consistency models: linearizability, sequential, causal, eventual
CAP theorem (precisely, during partitions) and PACELC (latency vs consistency otherwise)
Consensus: why it's needed (leader election, locks); Raft at a high level (terms, elections, log replication); etcd and ZooKeeper as consensus stores
Distributed transactions: two-phase commit and its problems; sagas (choreography vs orchestration) with compensating actions
Event-driven architecture: events vs commands, event sourcing, CQRS (when they're worth it)
Reliability patterns: timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, idempotency (Week 16), dead letter queues (Week 20)
Monolith vs microservices; the modular monolith; service boundaries (domain-driven design basics: bounded contexts)

niche: Retry storms amplifying outages
Fencing tokens for safe distributed locks
The fallacies of distributed computing
Exactly-once processing as idempotency + deduplication

Type conversion: widening (automatic), narrowing (casts), overflow
var (local type inference)

The method

4. Order of computation
5. Answer location
Top-down (memoization with recursion) vs bottom-up (tabulation)
Space optimization (keeping only the last few states)

mainGroups.title: Computers, OS, Linux, Git, Networks (Weeks 1-7)

mainGroups.goal: you can build a production-shaped API and explain what happens inside Node and inside the database for every request. The main book for this phase is Designing Data- Intensive Applications (DDIA) by Martin Kleppmann; get it now (2nd edition if available).

mainGroups.title: System Design and Capstone (Weeks 33-36)
